summary: Describes how the LDAP authPassword attribute can store the secrets used by the SCRAM authentication mechanism in SASL. This lets a directory hold the data a server needs to verify SCRAM logins. It is informational.

eli5.summary: It tells a phone-book-style database how to safely store what it needs to check a secret puzzle answer.

questions: how to store scram secrets in ldap
subtitle: How an LDAP directory can store the secrets a server needs to check SCRAM logins.

tldr.problem: A server that verifies SCRAM logins needs stored per-user secrets, and an LDAP directory needed a defined way to hold them.
tldr.mechanism: The existing authPassword attribute carries the SCRAM mechanism name, the iteration count and salt, and the StoredKey and ServerKey, each in a defined layout.
tldr.outcome: The values must be protected as if they were cleartext passwords, and servers must validate the format before use.

today: RFC 5803 is an Informational RFC published in July 2010. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What the RFC Defines
sections.content:
RFC 5803 describes how the authPassword LDAP attribute, defined in RFC 3112, can store the secrets used by the SCRAM SASL mechanisms from RFC 5802.

The attribute is multivalued, so one entry may hold several SCRAM values, for example for different hashing algorithms.
sections.eli5: A directory already has a drawer for password-like items. This note says what to put in it for the secret-puzzle login.

sections.title: How the Attribute Is Filled In
sections.content:
The scheme part is the SCRAM mechanism name, always without the -PLUS suffix, for example SCRAM-SHA-1. The authInfo part is the iteration count, then :, then the base64-encoded salt.

The authValue part is the base64-encoded StoredKey, then :, then the base64-encoded ServerKey. The iteration count is a positive number without leading zeros. The RFC gives the grammar in ABNF.
sections.eli5: Each record has a label for the recipe, a note on how many times it was mixed and the salt used, and two scrambled keys. Colons separate the pieces.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security considerations of SCRAM and its hash functions also apply, as do those of authPassword. The values SHOULD be protected as if they were cleartext passwords.

A read of the attribute not protected by a privacy layer such as IPsec or TLS can let an attacker impersonate the user to servers using the same hash function, password, iteration count and salt, or run an offline dictionary or brute-force attack to recover the password.

Servers MUST validate the format of the attribute before using it. The RFC names big iteration counts and invalid base64 encoding as two possible exploits.
sections.eli5: Even scrambled secrets are valuable, so guard them like the real password and double-check a record looks right before using it.

data.title: authPassword parts for SCRAM
data.code:
scram-authInfo  = iter-count ":" salt
scram-authValue = stored-key ":" server-key
iter-count      = %x31-39 *DIGIT

references.text: Zeilenga, K., "LDAP Authentication Password Schema", RFC 3112, May 2001.
Menon-Sen, A., Newman, C., Melnikov, A., and N. Williams, "Salted Challenge Response Authentication Message (SCRAM) SASL Mechanisms", RFC 5802, July 2010.
Melnikov, A. and K. Zeilenga, "Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL)", RFC 4422, June 2006.
